speakeroldname: Mr. C. H. CAHAN (St. Lawrence-St. George):
maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS
subsubtopic: DEBATE ON ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, when the leader of
the opposition (Mr. Bennett) invited me to reply to the address on the budget of the Minister of Finance (Mr. Robb), I could not but accept the invitation as an expression of personal confidence and goodwill on his part; but the task of replying to that address and of setting forth as best I can the views and policy of the Conservative party in this house and in the country on the several matters enunciated by the Minister of Finance is, I find, a grave duty and responsibility and, therefore, I ask the indulgence of the house when I attempt to perform that duty.
The Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) in a recent debate endeavoured, as he

frequently does, to distinguish between the expressions "equality of status" and "differences of functions." I presume he will not disagree with me in the suggestion that hon. members on this side of the house have an equality of status with members of the government and their supporters on the other side. The difference of function is one which, I think, he will also admit. We have had from the government from time to time the expression of their function in giving a very incomplete statement of the facts relating to the administration of the government and the financial and commercial conditions of the country. After the Minister of Finance has presented his budget, in which he confines himself to the truth but to a very incomplete statement of the truth, it is always necessary that members on this side should fulfil their onerous duty of placing the full facts before the country.
I notice that on the very evening on which the Minister of Finance made his budget speech, another gentleman, who is very prominent indeed, or who wishes to be so, in the public life of this country, made a speech in the city of Montreal in which he claimed for himself and one or two of his associates the full responsibility, and corresponding gratitude of the public, for all the advantageous results which the Minister of Finance had noted. I do not know and I cannot judge from personal knowledge of the capacity of Sir Henry Thornton as an administrator of the railways of this country, but apparently he thinks that the Prime Minister, the Finance minister and the Minister of Railways are mere binary -satellites who become known to the public only when they stand in the reflected light of his great -sun or star. But in this house we must look to the ministers of the government, who have assumed the responsibility of the administration of public affairs in Canada for a statement and explanation of their conduct in the administration of their respective offices, and I think the government and parliament and the people of this country would be better satisfied if Sir Henry Thornton would not so often obtrude himself into matters of which he has only a partial knowledge and no experience whatever.
The Finance minister, in making his statement to the house, dealt with the net debt of the country, and, simply because Sir Henry Thornton has obtruded himself into this public discussion, I intend to reflect somewhat upon the part he plays in the administration and in respect of the net and gross liabilities of this country.

The Budget-Mr. Cahan
The net debt of Canada on March 31, 1927, was $2,347,834,370, showing on the face of the accounts a reduction of $41,896,729.33 in the net debt over that of the preceding year. And yet the national railway indebtedness, to the public only, increased in 1927 by $46,000,000.
The certificate of the firm of chartered accountants who have been employed for the first time by the finance minister to give a certificate as to the actual financial condition of the country, and who have audited the public accounts for the first time, contains the following:
We certify that the balance sheet has been compiled in a manner similar to the corresponding statements of previous years, and does not include in the net debt of the Dominion issues of the Canadian National Railway Company and companies included in its system, which carry the guarantee of the Dominion. The details of such guarantees are shown separately in the public accounts.
That I think is the first time that that specific statement has been placed in the return of the public accounts, and on that account it is interesting to note that the chartered accountants who have now for the first time audited the public accounts found it necessary in the fulfilment of their duty and responsibility to make that specific explanation.
The long term indebtedness of the Canadian National railways in respect of securities issued to and now held by the public amounted on December 31st last to $981,381,796 according to unrevised figures, but I assume they are approximately correct. A large portion of these securities are actually guaranteed as to principal and interest by the government; another portion are guaranteed as to interest only; but whether guaranteed or not, this government and the people of this country must accept full responsibility, morally and legally, for paying ultimately those liabilities; because, although they are kept in a separate account and are the liabilities of what I may term one branch of government, they are nevertheless the liabilities of the people of this country and ultimately must be paid by them. But the entire sum of $981,381,796, no part of which can ever be repudiated by this government, is not included to the extent of one dollar in the net debt of Canada as presented to parliament by the Finance minister in his budget speech.
The liability of the national railway system to the Dominion government for cash advances made out of the Dominion treasury on December 31, 1926-I have not the figures
for December 31, 1927, but they will no doubt be given by the Minister of Railways- amounted to $507,848,511. It would be expedient, I think, on another occasion that the Minister of Railways Should bring down his returns to this house so that they may be discussed in connection with the budget of the Finance minister with which they are intimately related. But let me remark that of this enormous sum of cash advances made by the government to the Canadian National railways not one dollar of interest has ever been paid. Only simple interest is computed thereon, and the simple interest up to December 31, 1927-1 have not the exact returns before me-undoubtedly amounted approximately $226,500,000. In addition there is included, I may say by way of explanation, certain other amounts to which I have made no reference whatsoever. There is included in the long term indebtedness of the national railway, as shown by the balance sheet of the company, about $436,500,000, which represents approximately the amount expended by the Canadian government upon certain government railway lines, such as the Intercolonial, the Prince Edward Island railway, eastern branch lines, and the Transcontinental railway, which entered into the consolidation of the national railway system. That is another amount which is entirely excluded and which may properly be placed, as the Minister of Railways has contended once in my hearing in this house, in a different category from those cash advances to the amount of $507,848,500 which had been made by the Dominion government to the railway company itself up to December 31, 1926.
I may add that on December 31, 1927, the long term indebtedness of the Canadian National railways to the investing public was, as already stated, $981,381,796. The long term indebtedness to the Dominion government, subject to the explanation which I have made, was $1,225,046,995, including, as I say, the cash advances amounting to $436,500,000- and the total long term indebtedness amounted, on December 31, 1927, according to the unrevised report to which I have had access, to $2,236,428,791. I submit, Mr. Speaker, that those figures are sufficiently staggering to have received some comment and explanation from the minister who presides over the Department of Finance.	_	_
Now, the minister also laid claim to reductions in the net debt. He stated, according to the report tabled', that the net debt of Canada was actually reduced by $41,896,729, for the fiscal year 1926-27. That is true in the restricted sense that the accounts of the Department of Finance actually showed such
The Budget-Mr. Cahan

a reduction in the net debt. But there is this other department or branch of government, namely, the Canadian National railways, whose liabilities, as I have already said, and as I wish to emphasize, are not included in that statement of the Finance minister. When the Finance minister, therefore, reported a net reduction in the debt for the fiscal yeai ending March 31, 1927, if I remember, of $41,896,729, he failed to take into consideration the increases in the long term liabilities of that other branch of government to which I have called attention, which, during the calendar year ending December 31st last, increased its long term liabilities to the public-let me confine it to that, excluding its debt to the government for public advances-increased its long term public debt from $935,383,109 on December 31st, 1926, to $981,381,796, on December 31st last, an increase for the year of $45,998,697, approximately $46,000,000, in the net debt to the public on account of the railway alone, as compared with a decrease of $41,900,000 in the debt to the public of those other branches of government over which the Finance minister presides. When the minister made that statement of decrease in the public debt there was loud applause on the other side of the house. I fail to hear any applause from the other side now.

speechtext:
Far from being the whole

The Finance Minister and some of his journalistic supporters throughout the country, when members on this side of the house, in attempting a solution of any public problem, present the whole truth, regard it as an unpatriotic action. I have only to say, with the best of goodwill to the Prime Minister and those who surround him, that I and other members on this side are not unwilling to enter into a comparison with him and his associates at any time and on any occasion with respect to the performance of our patriotic duty, and I may add that we on this side have as much disinterested loyally to the best interests of this country as the Prime Minister or any other hon. member, even his most humble supporter or journalistic advocate.

The Prime Minister reported also a reduction in the net debt of Canada during the four years from March 31, 1923, if I have the figures correctly, to March 31, 1927, of $105,-942,498.65-he was particular even to the sixty-five cents. That statement was also true in a restricted sense, but it was not the whole truth in respect of the reduction or increase of the liabilities of the government and of the people of this country. The fact is that the long term debt of the national railways to the public, excluding the original appropriations for the construction of the government lines, excluding the advances made in cash by the government to the national railway system, excluding the simple interest which has accrued on those cash advances-excluding all those things, the net debt of the national railways to the public alone, which amounted on December 31, 1923, to $823,099,056, was increased on December 31st, 1927, to $981,381,796, an increase of net indebtedness to the public in that time of $158,282,740, as compared with a decrease of $105,942,498 which the Finance minister showed in respect of the departments whose accounts he calculated in his return. If all the governmental accounts were kept as they should be, and the liabilities shown as they should be in the financial statement which the Minister of Finance annually submits to parliament, he would not have been able to announce a reduction in the debt in those five years of $105,942,498; he would have had to announce an increase in the net debt of the country during the same time of $52,340,000, on account of the increasing net liabilities of the government to the investing public during the four years mentioned.

On a proper basis of accounting the $65,000,000 of bonds which, as the Finance minister discloses, were issued by the Canadian National Railways as of July 1, 1927, guaranteed by the Government of Canada, would have appeared as a direct liability of the Government of Canada.
But these bonds do not, by the present system of accounting, appear as part of the consolidated debt, nor as a part of the net debt of Canada, although on January 1 last $60,272,764 of the proceeds of this loan had been expended-an amount which more than wipes out the Finance minister's estimate of $38,815,000 as the prospective reduction of the net debt during the year ending March 31, next.

The Budget-Mr. Cahan
The Finance minister continued:
It is with pleasure and satisfaction that once again we are in a position to propose further reductions in taxation.
He was not speaking of the rate of taxation. He was giving the impression-I think deliberately-to this parliament and to the people that there had been great reductions in the volume of taxation from year to year under the Liberal administration. He might have added, even in giving his own partial description of the facts for the sake of better clarity and greater verity, that the sales tax and income tax reductions-both reductions of special war taxes-were in fact reductions merely in increases of taxation which this government had previously imposed. They found the sales tax levied at the rate of 3 per cent; they increased it to 6 per cent. They then discovered that this rate was an intolerable burden on the country, increasing exorbitantly, as every per cent of it did, the cost of living. They first reduced it to 5 per cent, then to 4 per cent, and now they propose to reduce it to 3 per cent-just where they found it on attaining office. I think the opinion on both sides of the house is that when making their last reduction they should have announced the abolition of this tax, for thereby they would have done more than by any other single act of government to reduce the average cost of living in this country, which is so high in comparison with the cost of living in the same state of society across the border. They increased, two years ago, the income tax so as to impose double taxation on the incomes of all companies- once on the incomes as earned, and again upon the same incomes when distributed. Now, in a round about way-and apparently this government can never do anything frankly and directly-they propose to mitigate in some degree the burdens which they themselves had previously imposed, and which the people have found almost intolerable.
But apart from decreases in their own impositions of taxes, the volume of taxation has not been diminished since the Liberal party took office away back in 1921. In 1924 their excise taxes increased from $107,989,893 in 1923 to 1123,668,847. In 1925, by reductions made of their own increase of taxation, the excise tax was reduced to 889,330,838-a decrease of $34,338,009 below 1924. Between 1924 and 1925 there was some reduction in the amount collected of other war taxes which were imposed by ohem-selves. But, as I said before, except in these instances there has been no reduction in the volume of taxation annually collected. The total taxation collected rose from 409 millions in 1922 to 459 millions in 1923, to 479 millions in 1924. The total taxation then decreased by reason of the reduction in the taxes which they had previously imposed, and in 1925 the volume decreased to 395 millions. But the returns show that the amount of taxation increased next year to 443 millions, and again in 1927 to 471 millions. In the fiscal year 1927, which should have showed such enormous reductions in taxation according to the statement of the Minister of Finance, they obtained from taxation 61 millions of dollars more than in 1922, their first year of office.
I ask the indulgence of the house to place on Hansard a short statement, which may be examined by hon. gentlemen on both sides of the house, showing how these increases took place in the four years which I have briefly reviewed.

Certain changes in the tariff and in the tariff policy of the country have been announced in this budget. Before proceeding to discuss these items, many of which are exceedingly difficult of discussion inasmuch as they call for a great deal of technical knowledge and skill, I wish to state what I believe to be the general tariff policy of the Conservative party in this house and in the country. We approve of tariff changes and generally of such tariff changes from time to time as the changing conditions of domestic industry and of foreign trade may require. In effecting such revision and the correlative readjustment of tariff rates we on this side
Total..

The Budget-Mr. Cahan
of the house stand by certain principles. These principles I intend to enumerate as best I can:
1.	The stimulating and developing of our vast and varied natural resources.
2.	The preservation and enlargement of the markets at home and abroad for Canadian farm products.
3.	The 'establishment, extension and development of Canadian industries on stable and remunerative bases, so as to induce investments in Canada, of Canadian as well as foreign funds, and particularly so as to create and furnish such ever-extending and diversified employment to the Canadian people as will preclude any considerable emigration of Canadians to the United States of America for the purpose of seeking more remunerative employment in that country.
4.	The stabilization in Canada of the costs of living and the costs of implements of production on such comparatively low bases as will enable our people, in producing and selling our surplus of national products abroad, to compete advantageously with the products of foreign countries in our common markets abroad.
5.	The reduction of the customs tariff or the imposition of higher excise taxes, whenever and wherever necessary, to prevent the immoral use or abuse of the existing tariff, or any unfair advantage being taken of the tariff, as for example by those who would resort to profiteering by exacting unduly high prices for their products from domestic consumers, under the protecting elements of the existing tariff.
6.	The adjustment from time to time of our preferential treatment of the products of the British countries comprised within the British commonwealth of nations, so as to modify preferences which are given at the expense of the Canadian farmer, dairyman or other industrial worker, and which tend to restrict domestic employment and decrease the general standards of living in this country; and
7.	The promotion of the export and import trade of Canadian ports wherever possible.
This I understand to be a general statement, in my unexpressive language, of the tariff policy of the Conservative party in this house and in the country. We fully realize that in such a widely extended country as the Dominion of Canada the economic independence of any one section or of any one group or class is an unrealizable dream. We realize that each section and group are dependent upon each other section and group for the promotion of our common interests. We must
stand or fall together in this country. No one section of Canada can suffer permanent injury without detriment to the whole body politic. In a word, we cannot conserve the economic interests of the whole country by promoting exclusively the interests of any one group or class. No one section of the country should be permitted to seek its sole aggrandizement at the expense of the whole body politic.
We recognize also that the monopoly of either trade or industry is often-times a source of economic evil, and, when such tendencies become manifest, they must, like every other public evil, be subjected to the control and restraint of this parliament. But we remember, and we affirm, that unfair and dishonest foreign competition is also prejudicial to the producers of this country, and measures for its due restraint are in like manner necessary and commendable. In every such case, however, such measures should be conceived and carried into effect for the general public interest of Canada, and not for the aggrandizement and profit of any particular group or class, no matter how closely associated they may be to the government of the country.
Experience has disclosed that each group or class or section of the country will tend to govern in its own interests when it has the opportunity and is irresponsible; but members of this parliament, on either side of the house, are, I suggest, representative of the whole Canadian nation, and as such they must exercise their authority without fear or favour in the interests of the Dominion as a whole.
The national policy as formulated by Conservative statesmen was designed, and admittedly designed, for the political unification and for the material and economic development of the whole country. Readjustments of the customs tariff for the encouragement of domestic industry were advocated only as one of the several elements of that policy. The national policy, in its broad outlines, contemplated the extension of the dominion from sea to sea; the opening up of the northern half of this continent to trade, traffic and transportation by railways and canals; the building of wharves and docks for the increase of commercial and shipping facilities; the intensive encouragement, on an extensive scale, of such primary industries as agriculture, forestry, mining and fishing; and, since men and women cannot live by bread alone, the national policy contemplated the establishment and extension in Canada of secondary
The Budget-Mr. Cahan

industries suitable to the existing conditions of this country, which will supply, so far as reasonably possible, the multifarious equipment, clothing, furniture, utensils and other things which satisfy the needs of our daily life. There are thousands of our own people who are not well adapted for the work of our primary industries of agriculture, mining, forestry and fisheries, and it is therefore necessary, if we would conserve the interests of the whole country, that we should establish from time to time those industries suitable to our necessities which will enable large classes of our people to obtain and retain employment in Canada, where they may contribute by their skill and labour to the economic welfare and advancement of our own country. The development of our primary industries being assured and safeguarded, the men who by their skill and labour in our domestic factories transform the raw materials of leather into boots and shoes, of coal and iron ore into iron and steel products, of wood pulp into paper, of wool into clothing and the like, are creating
national wealth and promoting the general prosperity of the Canadian people. The secondary industries we maintain should be encouraged. But we must ever bear in mind that there can be nothing final in the political, industrial and commercial development of a widely extended country such as ours, which is only partly prospected, only partly explored, and its future progress and prosperity must depend upon our loyal, and sometimes our self-sacrificing, cooperation foe the attainment of ends which we all have in common.
I obtained from the department of statistics a statement of the industrial production of Canada for the year 1926, and to save the time which would be consumed in reading it I ask leave now to have it inscribed upon Hansard.

In the end they increased the net protection by reducing the tariff on materials and component parts imported, and also by reducing the sales tax previously imposed on the Canadian product, so as practically to maintain the same net protection and thus permit the Canadian industry to survive. I refer to that because I find the same tactics exemplified in the tariff schedules which have been submitted in the budget for the approval of parliament. But would not an intelligent public-because while you may deceive some of the people some of the time you cannot deceive all of the people all of the time-have more respect for the Minister of Finance and the government which he represents, if he did not resort to this sort of camouflage, but had the courage frankly to admit that by this indirect method he was endeavouring to please both wings of the divided party on which the maintenance of the government in power depends? In the end it is the producers of wool, hemp, iron and steel, and other primary Canadian products who suffeT, and as a result of this and similar reductions of duties on raw materials, we find that Canadian growers of wool, dairy producers, and coal, iron and steel producers, are placed under serious disabilities, while their employees from year to year, as I will endeavour to show, are forced to emigrate and seek employment in the republic to the south.

Some Canadian mills may receive from some items of drawback or some items of customs duty a slight advantage as, for example, in the advance of duty on textiles of cotton mixed with rayon or on pure rayon textiles. Other mills, such as Wabasso, which confine themselves to particular branches of the trade, may reap some slight benefit from some of the changes made. Penmans will probably not be prejudicially affected so far as my vision goes, but I am not an expert. But the Minister of Finance, referring to these cotton schedules of the new tariff, said1:
Coupled with the general lowering of rates on the finished products is a lowering of rates on yarns and other materials used by manufacturers for further processes.
There we have the automobile trick all played over again, the second time in an attempt to appease the conflicting elements which I see on the opposite side of the house. This statement tends to create in the minds of one wing the impression that the customs duties have been lowered all along the line, and in the minds of the other that the net protection to the manufacturer has been maintained. But, continuing, the Minister of Finance said:
In the proposed changes the needs of the Canadian consumer and manufacturer have been carefully considered, while incidentally the scope of the British preference has been materially widened.
Let me deal for a moment with the alleged widening of the scope of the British preference in respect of cotton fabrics. Four items of the new tariff, namely: 523, 523a, 523b and 523c cover all imports of cotton woven fabrics. Item 523a remains unchanged, evidently, as I think, and as I may suggest, for the purpose of quieting some friends of the administration who probably have special and irresistible claims. Consider first the British preference as shown in these four items. In item 523 the British preferential rate is 12i per cent; no change. In item 523a the British preferential rate is 15 per cent; no change. In item 523b the old British preferential rate of 22i per cent is reduced to 20 per cent-a reduction of 2i per cent. In item 523c the old British preferential rate of 22J per cent is reduced to 20 per cent-a reduction of 2i per cent.

The whole problem of immigration, to which this parliament is asked to-day to give special attention by sending a resolution on the question to the standing committee on agriculture and colonization,-I say, the solution of the whole problem of immigration into this country and of emigration from this country depends upon one thing and one thing only:	It depends in the final analysis

This is the problem which, from year to year, confronts the hon. gentleman who sits in the office of Minister of Finance. But it is a problem to which he appears not to have given the slightest possible attention. He comes to this house year after year and tells us of the enormous development of our import trade, while year by year our own factories are idle, our own industries are diminishing and our Canadian workmen are being driven out of employment, and while, year by year, we are giving to American factories, which have the advantage of selling their manufactures in their larger market, the privilege of controlling the markets of Canada as well. If hon. gentlemen opposite intend to fulfil their whole duty and responsibility of promoting the advancement and progress of the country which Providence has committed to our charge, they cannot overlook, they must not overlook, the absolute necessity of providing more varied and more extended employment for our people. This is a matter that comes home to my heart because, wdiile I sit in my office in Montreal,, month after month I am besieged by young men from the technical colleges and the universities, young men who have served their time in our industrial concerns, who cry, "For goodness sake, Mr. Cahan, can you not find employment for us in this country-this country in which we were bom and bred?" And what can I do? I have to tell them that I am utterly incapable of doing anything to help them under present conditions, with the result that they take the night trains for the United States and enter into industry there. I tell hon. gentlemen that in a country such as ours, with our large agricultural industry, which is growing from year to year, and with our industrial development, depressed though it is, there should not be one native-jborn Canadian who could not to-morrow or a week hence find profitable employment somewhere in this Dominion in some of our diversified industries. Until hon. gentlemen give to this problem the attention which it demands, and find a solution, we
The Budget-Mr. Cahan

shall never have the development of Canada placed on a permanent, stable 'basis. Until they solve this problem of unemployment we shall simply be raising families of sons and daughters and educating them here at our expense to qualify them to take up their vocations for life in the neighbouring republic.
Providence has committed to our charge and responsibility, temporarily under this government, one of the finest countries ever created, and we are making such a mess of the administration of it that we cannot retain our own people at home nor, without paying millions in bonuses, induce people even from the starved areas of Europe to come here and settle and make their permanent homes here. I therefore ask leave, Mr. Speaker, to move in amendment, seconded by the hon. the leader of the opposition (Mr. Bennett):
That all the words after the word "that" be struck out and the following substituted therefor:
This house regrets that the measures proposed by the government do not tend to provide increased employment in Canada, nor to induce the return of Canadians to their native land, nor to prevent the continued emigration of our people to the United States; and that they make no provisions for the preservation of our domestic markets for Canadian farm and dairy products, nor for the effective development of the natural resources of the country, nor for the abolition of the sales tax by the 1st of January 1928-
That is wrong; I should have read, " 1929."

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as, unlike the hon. member for St. Lawrence-St. George (Mr. Cahan), my time is limited to forty minutes, I shall not endeavour to emulate his exhaustive analysis of the budget proposals, nor is it my intention to comment in any way upon his address. With some of the remarks he has made in a most excellent, address I am in entire accord. To some I might take exception. But I shall say nothing further than this:
I listened with intense interest while the hon. member indicated and outlined the tariff policy of the Conservative party as laid down at the convention in Winnipeg last October. I think that it warrants the term which is used in that connection. For years we have listened to a plea for stability in tariff matters. Now "flexibility" has taken 
its place, and I gathered from the hon. gentleman's remarks, as I followed his interpretation of the policy, that it provided for these things: for the manufacturer it suggested "adequate protection" without using the words; to the farmer "low cost of production"; to labour "steady employment at remunerative wages"; and to the consumer in general "protection against exploitation and increase in the cost of living." I can only say, Mr. Speaker, that if any tariff policy could bring about all these beneficial results I think the country as a whole would welcome it, and would adopt it as a truly national policy. The thought was in my mind, as I listened to his speech, and as I remembered some statements made by the present Prime Minister in former days, that the Conservatives at the present time have apparently adopted in toto the fiscal policy of the premier at that time; and I can only hope that what is suggested in some parts of the present budget proposals is not true, and that the Liberal party have not adopted as their policy the former policy of the Conservatives.
Mr. Speaker, in endeavouring to consider for a few moments the budget proposals brought down by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Robb), my first words must be words of congratulation to the minister for the manner of its presentation. It was brief and concise, characterized by clarity of expression and by an absence of cumbrous or unnecessary verbiage. It was characterized also by a refreshing absence of overmuch political boasting. I may also congratulate him on one aspect at least of the budget itself. It illustrated the fact, which is well known to the people of Canada, that not only is the minister a capable business man- and as such respected throughout this Dominion-but that he is also a diplomat and a politician of a very high order. To my mind, Mr. Speaker, this budget represents a clever and not unsuccessful attempt to reconcile and express the varying and conflicting interests and opinions which go to form the present Liberal party. To the one wing we find is offered a reduced income tax; to our manufacturers a lowering of tariff on some of the raw materials which enter into the goods that they manufacture; to the other wing we find a reduction of the sales tax offered and, I am free to say, a rather vague and indefinite suggestion of a general revision of the tariff. I hold, Mr. Speaker, that it is a clever and not unsuccessful attempt to reconcile all the varying opinions upon which the minister must depend for support.

The Budget-Mr. Speakman
I wish to consider for a moment the preamble to the budget itself. That preamble includes two statements of some moment. The first is the following which I quote:
Seldom have the annual statements from leaders of finance and industry throughout Canada so generally reflected such progress and prosperity as that of the year 1927.
Mr. Speaker, the claim that we in this country are enjoying increased prosperity has frequently been made by successive ministers of finance, and not infrequently with less reason for the statement than exists at the present time. I can well believe that from the point of view of those leaders of finance and industry referred to by the minister the assertion is in this case indisputable. Undoubtedly there is an increase in the volume of business being done 'within this country, increased dividends are in many instances being paid, and our banks, trust and insurance companies are becoming the depositories, and to some degree the beneficiaries, of an increasing volume of wealth. This question, however, is being asked by hundreds of thousands of men and women in Canada to-day:	Why, in view
of these visible manifestations of increased wealth it is so difficult, in many cases so impossible, for individuals to secure any share of that wealth for their own personal requirements. While business is increasing and wealth accumulating, tens of thousands of our workmen throughout this country are in receipt ot a scale of wages far below the amount necessary to maintain a decent standard of living according to the computation of the Department of Labour. Thousands of our farmers are fighting to make ends meet, working under conditions and home surroundings which many of us here can not visualize, which none of us would tolerate, and content and satisfied if at the end of the year they have been able to hold their own. Moreover, hundreds of our small tradesmen and professional men throughout this country are struggling in that morass which has engulfed so many of their kind and forced them into bankruptcy. This question demands an answer. I cannot answer it, but I may suggest a line of inquiry which, if followed to the end by men more able than myself, might assist in the solution of this problem. The tendency of modern civilization is to concentrate our population in a few large centres, to centralize industrial production in large and larger units, and to concentrate the control of both industry and finance in the hands of a decreasing number of increasingly wealthy individuals and groups of individuals. In the
limited time at my disposal I have not the opportunity to discuss whether this system is unavoidable or not, or whether it is good or bad. I will say this however: That through a multitude of channels is drawn to these centres a large part of the profits made in this country by the industry of men and women throughout the whole countryside. On the' other hand the back channels through which these profits dhould again flow to irrigate the countryside, and freshen and brighten the lives of our people, seem to have been overlooked or are obstructed. Or to put the same thought into other words, centralization while it tends to efficiency in production, tends also to the most appalling inefficiency in distribution both of profits and of products. To solve this dual problem of distribution, possibly through cooperative effort, is a task towards which the best minds of the country both in the government and outside their ranks might well turn their serious and earnest attention.
Since I was a small boy I have worked on a farm or have been closely associated with men who have worked on and are working on farms, and I am inclined to believe that the same conditions which apply there apply largely to all classes of industries. We find men and women working day by day intelligently and industriously at hard manual labour; we find them very often working under admittedly unpleasant conditions, and we find them, in the case of the farmers at least, working for very long hours and yet apparently unable to provide for themselves and their families comfortable homes according to the modern standard of comfort, a decent comfortable standard of living and education, and some reserve in case of sickness or death. Why is that? It must be due to one of these two things. Is it because the workman as a whole, who is after all, in field and factory, in mine and forest, the great producer of our national wealth, receives an unfair remuneration for his work, or is it because he has to pay an unfair price for the things he has to purchase? One or other or both of these must be true, and due to my own circumstances during my life I have been face to face with that problem so that it has become a very real problem to me as it is to the people I represent. Again I would urge upon this house, regardless of any question of politics or parties, to concentrate on the problem of returning to the workingman of any sort, any class, whether manual or mental worker, a fair share of the wealth which he produces.

The Budget-Mr. Speakman
The next point in the preamble to which I should like to call attention is again an utterance of the minister. This is what he says:
The statement of the nation's business will show conclusively that, notwithstanding our annual reductions in the rate of taxation, our revenues have been ample to meet fixed charges, take care of the ever increasing needs of a growing country, and provide also for a reduction of debt.
As regards the first part of that statement as to reductions in taxation I concur in the ministers statement, and I am afraid I cannot follow the reasoning of the hon. member for St. Lawrence-St. George (Mr. Cahan) and some of his colleagues. After all the true test as to the weight of taxation is not the aggregate amount but the percentage of income or business profits which is drawn into the channels of taxation, and while it is true that a greater aggregate and a greater per capita amount have been paid in taxes, still it is also true that reductions have been made and that the percentage of taxation on profits made-and by profits I mean all income secured in any way at all-is slightly lessened. Let me illustrate what I mean in this way. Assuming for a moment that the price of motor cars has been reduced-and I think that is a fair assumption at the present time -and assuming that, partly by reason of that reduction in price, so many more cars are sold that the aggregate amount and the per capita amount paid for cars within the country are greater than before, no one would argue from that situation that the actual cost of motor cars had not been reduced. That is an illustration of what I mean when I say that it is the percentage, the rate, and not the aggregate amount that should be taken ino consideration in discussing the subject of tax reduction.
But I cannot agree with the next statement of the minister as to the debt reduction, and I find myself drawn to the same logical conclusion as that expressed by the hon. member for ISt. Lawrence-St. George and on former occasions by others in this house. I have not the time to go into t'he back history of this country and I will not burden Hansard with any intricate computations. I will say simply this:	We have in the same statement
side by side the declaration of the minister that, after allowing for certain reduced assets, the net reduction of our national debt will amount to $38,815,000, while at the same time and during the same year $65,000,000 worth of Canadian National railway bonds were guaranteed by the government. A portion of that guarantee was simply a refunding matter. 
An amount of some $20,000,000 indicates simply a change from a Short-term, three-year guaranteed obligation to a long-term, thirty-year guaranteed obligation. It is simply a matter Of bookkeeping and it neither adds to nor diminishes the total sum of our liabilities. The bulk, however, of the rest is a fresh liability on the part of the railways. I can conceive that if, as in the case of the Montreal harbour commission, for example, which had also guaranteed bonds to the extent of $S,000,000, the security within the company is ample to cover such bonds, the minister might say that it did not add to the liability of the country. But what are the facts in this case? It is generally believed and freely stated that the Canadian National Railways are at the present time over-capitalized. It is being suggested-and I concur in that suggestion-that the capital should be written down to a reasonable figure in order to allow them to have a fair Showing in competition with other similar lines. If the railway is over-capitalized, this means that every available asset and every form of security it offers are mortgaged more than one hundred per cent. It means that there is no security in the railway itself for any additional loans or obligations, and we are in the position of a man who signs a note for another man who is mortgaged to the extent of every stick of furniture he owns, who has no assets of his own to meet that obligation. In that and in this case the guarantor becomes in fact the debtor. I shall leave that as my time is short and I simply wish to indicate my opinion and give some reasons for it.
I commend very heartily the minister's action in reducing the sales tax by 25 per cent. It is a tax which is cumbersome in operation and unfair in application. It pyramids as it reaches the consumer and becomes greater. It affects directly the standard and the cost of living and it hampers business in general. I think it was a proper move for the minister to reduce that tax at least to the extent he has done.
When I come, however, to the tariff proposals I am somewhat at a loss. I am without the intimate knowledge of certain lines of business that is possessed by the hon. member for St. Lawrence-St. George, and in the absence of comparative schedules, which the minister will table and which will be at our disposal at a later time, I am unable to arrive at any accurate or detailed knowledge as to what that revision actually means. The reclassification is carried on to such a degree; items are carried from one classification to

The Budget-Mr. Speakman
another, and no comparative schedules are given showing the actual reduction or increase made that it is impossible for me to form anything but a general estimate as to the line which has been followed in that tariff revision. One or two indications, however, are fairly distinct and clear. The first is that a large portion at least of this reduction does not tend and was not intended to give any relief to the consumers, but was intended, so far as it is effective-and I am not discussing the question of its being effective-to give .manufacturers a little greater advantage by reducing some of the costs of the raw materials and the machinery which enter into the cost of the manufacture. With that I have no quarrel whatever. I am simply indicating what to my mind are the salient features of the budget. As to the general revision affecting consumers I shall say nothing; I am inclined to think the effect will be slight, but lacking accurate information I do not intend to give utterance to a premature opinion.
On one point, however, I am fairly clear, and that is the question of the British preference. The statement has been made that it has been amplified and enlarged. Again, I shall not follow the hon. member for St. Lawrence-St. George into his computations as to the exact meaning of the word. I wish to point out that accompanying the suggestion that the British preference is being amplified and enlarged comes the qualification that the percentage of the empire cost of production shall be increased from twenty-five to fifty per cent on all goods coming in under that preferential rate. Inevitably and obviously that provision will mean the effective curtailment of the quantity of goods coming in under that tariff. I am not saying that that is right or wrong; I am simply pointing out what would obviously be the effect. If you increase the percentage of empire cost of production from twenty-five to fifty per cent, you will inevitably curtail the quantity of goods coming in under that preferential tariff, and I cannot see how that can be called an amplifying or widening of the preferential idea.
There is another point in connection with the tariff to which I would like to refer, and that is in regard to the work of the advisory tariff board. Ever since my intelligence has led me to regard such a board as a fact-finding board, I have been in favour of it, but in view of the fact that the evidence brought before that board and the evidence elicited by it is not available to the members of this house, although it is available, I presume, to the government. I believe that the opinions of tho?" who hold that that board is a smoke
screen behind which the government can evade responsibility are at least partly justified. I took issue with that statement when it was first made because I conceived it to be a sound principle when we were dealing with the tariff that we should be in possession of all the information necessary to come to a conclusion, but if that information is to be only in the hands of the government and not in the possession of members of the house, then when the Minister of Finance says that the board has inquired into certain matters and certain findings have been made, I say that the government is to that extent shifting the responsibility from itself to the board, because it is not giving to the members of this house the opportunity to judge for themselves the value of the information brought forward. I urge upon the Minister of Finance that as soon as possible and at all events before another budget comes down an adequate appropriation be submitted to the house to provide for the perusal by members of parliament of the information brought before the tariff board to which they are entitled, and which they expected to receive when voting for its formation.
I come now, Mr. Speaker, to that part of the budget to which I take the greatest exception, and that is the reduction in the income tax, coupled with the statement by the minister that " it is proposed that the Dominion shall continue gradually to lighten the load in the income tax field ", There is an inescapable inference to be drawn from that language and from the action of the government in bringing down this budget, and that is that the Finance minister and the government contemplate the gradual elimination of this form of taxation. I do not take issue with that on the ground imputed to myself and some of my colleagues by the daily press and by some hon. members to my right, that we object to any reduction in this form of taxation because we and the men and women we represent do not pay income tax, not having sufficient income to come within the scope of the act. It is possible, I believe in this house, and I claim that right for myself as I accord it to others, to discuss questions on their merits, without either imputing or receiving imputations that we are speaking from a selfish point of view. I do not impute to any gentleman here who votes for a reduction in the income tax the motive that he is voting for it because he has a large income and is therefore personally interested in a reduction, and I personally expect to have my own opinion respected in like manner. I am
The Budget-Mr. Speakman

opposed to this reduction on grounds that I shall give which appear to me to be sound as applied to the whole country.
First, I would say that this tax, with others, was instituted as a war tax to take care of the increased expenditure of this country consequent upon the war. Is that expenditure done away with now? Is that debt paid? Is the debt for which the income tax was instituted retired to such an extent that we are warranted in eliminating the tax?

Mr.	HEAPS:	I	realize that,	but	weall know that it	is	nothing new	for thesethings	to appear	in	print before	they	areactually brought up in the house. I have been informed on reliable authority that speeches have appeared in the Montreal newspapers before	they were	actually delivered in	the
House of Commons here. However, in continuing this discussion I should like to 6ay that I was very much interested in the opening remarks of the Minister of Finance (Mr. Robb) when introducing his budget. He said:
Mr. Speaker, seldom have the annual statements from leaders of finance and industry throughout Canada so generally reflected such progress and prosperity as that of the year 1927.
I wonder why, in that statement, the minister left out any allusion to the farmers and the labourers of this country. Surely they should be in the minister's mind when framing a budget for the people of the Dominion of Canada; yet he referred only to the progress as reflected by the statements of the leaders of finance and industry. If I were a leader of finance or industry I know I should regard the budget as being very good, but not
The Budget-Mr. Heaps

being such a leader I cannot say that. I represent a working class constituency, where most of the men and women have to work for the money they get, and they cannot be classed in any way in that particular category referred to. Consequently I am compelled to view the budget as it affects the electors whom I represent, and I think that is the attitude which should be taken by every hon. member of this house in discussing this question. I presume that one of the reasons why the minister did not refer to anyone with the exception of leaders of industry and finance s because no one else has enjoyed prosperity.

speechtext:
I will not put it as baldly
as that; I think there may be other reasons, because after the statements made in this house by the Minister of Immigration (Mr. Forke) and by others coming from farming communities, the minister might have known that he could not claim any prosperity among the farmers and workers of this country. Knowing that certain of the provincial governments had made requests for federal assistance to the unemployed, he must acknowledge that there is no prosperity among the workers here. From his opening statement I think it quite proper to infer that our farmers and workers were in no way prosperous during 1927. I admit there is a certain amount of prosperity in the country at the present time, but that prosperity is all at the top; it does not reflect itself at the bottom. What is prosperity? The fact that a bank manager, a railway president, or an industrialist, at an annual meeting, states that his particular institution has had a prosperous year is in my opinion no indication as to conditions throughout the country as a whole.
I think prosperity reflects itself in the general condition of the masses, and when they are prosperous in Canada, then, and1 only then, can it be truly said that we are in a state of prosperity. At the present time there is not an hon. member, I do not care from what part of the country he comes, who can say that the masses of the people are experiencing prosperity; and so long as they are in a state bordering on poverty, only a few days removed from starvation, perhaps not even knowing where their next meal is coming from, I think it well that we should hear less talk of prosperity and should consider the actual conditions as we find them throughout the Dominion.
I want, now, Mr. Speaker, to deal for a few moments with another condition of 
affairs in which the minister took a certain amount of pride. He referred to our huge exports and their excess over imports. People are very easily deluded when figures of that nature are placed before them. I do not attach any great importance to such figures It is quite true that in the past few years we have been exporting far more than we have been importing. I think one of the reasons for this is that we have in the past imported so much capital that we are now repaying in goods some of our borrowings. I am using now the minister's own arguments in his budget speech. He claimed that in 1913 Canada had an adverse balance of trade of $29.61 per capita, and that in the same year India had a favourable trade balance. Now, because of that favourable trade balance does he mean to say that the people of India in 1913 were in a better condition than the people of this Dominion? That is the inference one must draw from the statement he placed on Hansard. Of course, it only goes to show the absurdity of trying to arrive at conclusions respecting the actual condition of a country by discussing the question of favourable or unfavourable trade balances. Invisible imports and exports have always to be taken into consideration, but the Minister of Finance omitted-conveniently or inconveniently-to mention this feature. In this house we have a number of farmer members, and I heard them applaud the statement that our exports were greater than our imports.

speechtext:
Supposing a farmer has a
couple of hundred head of cattle and sells 150: if he had been compelled by force of circumstances to get rid of his cattle would he be proud of the fact? I do not think any farmer would be pleased with a situation of that character. Having by necessity been compelled to dispose of the greater portion of his stock, probably at an inadequate price by reason of the forced sale, he would not at all feel happy. The parallel holds good nationally. We have in this country vast natural resources-natural resources which, I believe, ought to be the inheritance of our people. What have we done? We have bartered away many of those resources for a mere pittance. The result of that is shown

The Budget-Mr. Heaps
to-day in exports. In the past few years we have imported a vast amount of American capital; I do not know exactly how many hundreds of millions of dollars have been invested by American capitalists in the water powers and forest wealth of this country. As a result development is following along lines that obtain in the United States-we find "company" towns springing up. Recently, Mr. Speaker, I was at a meeting of the Montreal Trades and Labour Council, and I heard men state that when they had gone to these company towns in the neighbouring province, created by the importation of American capital, they were refused admittance. In other words, the Canadian people are denied the right to set foot on Canadian soil, controlled by American capital. What applies in some parts of Quebec also applies, as I know, in certain parts of Manitoba.
I wish also to deal with the implications that follow the importation of this capital from the United States. I am not one of those who look with kindly feelings towards American imperialism, especially as I see its workings and its implications in Mexico and Nicaragua. I have read statements of United States ministers, high up in the councils of their government, in which they claim that American capital wherever invested is entitled to the protection of the American government. That is a new international doctrine. The other night we listened to the hon. leader of the opposition (Mr. Bennett) discuss the diversion of water from lake Michigan by the Chicago drainage authorities, and in the course of his speech he quoted a statement by the late President Roosevelt in connection with the Alaska boundary. The very same problem is intensified to-day when we look at the amount of United States capital invested in foreign countries. You will generally find that those investments are followed later on by United States military occupation. I do not suggest for a moment that after the capitalists of the United States have secured financial and industrial control of a large part of the Dominion their government is going to do the same in this country as they have done in some of the South American republics, but the implications are there. Only in to-day's newspapers we read that some of the highest authorities in the United States claim the right for their government to intervene wherever American investments may be jeopardized. There is no telling when we may pass laws that may not be altogether to the liking of those to the south of us, and under such circumstances I can see us getting into a nasty squabble with the government at Washington. So long as we have American capital coming here I do not see how we can possibly avoid it. For my part, I would far sooner have waited a little longer, if possible, for the development of our natural resources than see the people of Canada become, in the language of the Bible, hewers of wood and drawers of water to American capitalists.
At six o'clock the house took recess.
After Recess
The house resumed at eight o'clock.

speechtext:
When the house rose at six
o'clock I had just referred to the establishment by American capitalists of company towns in Canada. I do not mean it to be inferred from anything I have to say with respect to American capitalists that the Canadian capitalist is by any means a saint. However, the creation in this country of these company towns is something new, and something which I look upon with a great deal of disfavour. The men employed by these companies hardly dare call their souls their own. They are almost enslaved body and soul for a wage of from 35 to 45 cents per hour, and Canadians who attempt to enter these places are often prevented from doing so in spite of the fact that they are natives of this country.
The minister has reduced the income tax. By the reduction of that tax he is giving to these corporations an advantage which I do not think they are entitled to receive. It has been stated over the last week end, that the persons objecting to reduction of the income tax are those who do not pay that tax. I want to take issue with that statement. All taxation is paid out of production, and if there is no production there can be nothing to pay income tax with; and whilst it may be true that the farmer or the worker does not pay income tax directly, yet I claim that as they are the chief producers in the Dominion they thereby pay indirectly a large share of the income tax. I object to the reduction of the income tax because I believe it to be the fairest form of taxation. It is a tax that is based purely and simply upon ability to pay, and I do not think there is any fairer form of taxation than the taxation of those who have the ability to pay. The indirect taxation we have to-day places a heavy burden on the people of this country, and I would venture to assert that the farmer and

The Budget-Mr. Heaps
the worker pay heavier indirect taxes, in proportion to their income, than those who pay the income tax.
Now the Minister of Finance has been good enough to suggest in his speech, and I agree with the idea, that we ought not to shirk our responsibilities in regard to the national debt. He says that the people who created the debt ought not to shirk the payment of it, or words to that effect. I quite agree with that statement, but I maintain that the minister himself is shirking responsibility in reducing taxation and allowing the debt to remain at its present huge figure. He goes back to the year 1845, approximately eighty years ago, to try and find a precedent for the budget that he is bringing into this house in the year 1928. He quotes an economist who lived in that year in order to try and give the impression to this house and the country, that the budget he has brought in and the methods of financing he is adopting are the best that could be followed under modem circumstances. I entirely disagree with that premise. I believe myself that the minister ought to have a definite and fixed policy in regard to the payment of the national debt of Canada. There is no telling how long the national debt will remain the huge liability it is at present. He says we ought not to shirk our responsibility. Quite true, but how long did it take to create that debt? It was created in four years, and yet by the method of financing which is followed at present there is no way of telling whether the national debt will be paid in four years or in four hundred years. I believe that debt should be wiped out in as short a time as it took to create it. I have a suggestion to make to the minister and I hope he will give it due consideration. When I say "due consideration" I do not mean the kind of consideration which is frequently adopted by ministers when they throw suggestions into the waste paper basket.

You file them? Well, you do a little bit better than throwing them into the waste paper basket. As a matter of fact you file them so securely that you never can get at them again.
I would deal with this question of the national debt from a little different angle, perhaps, than the one from which hitherto it has been viewed. I am going to suggest to the government that the question of inflation and deflation as between the years 1920 and 1926, should, in some way, form a basis from which to consider the whole question of the national debt. In the first place no effort

has been made by this government to consider the problem of the national debt in relation to industry. In Great Britain a special commission was appointed in 1924 to consider this very important question, but in Canada we have allowed this matter to take care of itself by following purely haphazard methods; there has been no systematic or scientific effort on the part of the government to provide for the national debt of Canada. It is quite true that some reductions in our debt have been made during the past two or three years, yet these reductions cannot be regarded as the basis for a proper method of handling this problem. There is no such thing as a national sinking fund, and if lean years should come for the Dominion treasury it follows that no provision for reduction of the national debt could be made out of surplus revenue as is being done now. In 1920, and I am using that year because it was the peak year for commodity prices, our net debt was $2,248 868,624. At the end of the fiscal year, 1926, according to the Canada Year Book, our net debt was $2,389,731,099, showing an actual increase in the net debt for the year 1926 over the year 1920. It would not be fair to blame the government entirely for this condition. In 1920 there were shown assets of $792,660,963 which by 1926 had dwindled to $3/9,048,085, this dwindling of the national assets being to an extent due to the deflation which took place during that period. Whilst the government has very little to show because of this fact, the people of Canada have now to pay out of present production one hundred cents on the dollar which in 1920 was worth approximately 70 or 75 cents. The taxpayers of to-day and those of future generations are to be penalized in the first place for the inflation that took place in 1920 and in the second place for the deflation that took place in the period succeeding the inflation.
I want, however, to make this suggestion to the Minister of Finance. Most of the public debt of this Dominion was created during the period of inflated prices when the dollar was not worth what it is to-day. The following figures taken from the Canada Year Book will give the house some idea of the relative value of the dollar from 1900 to 1926. Taking the value of the dollar in 1913 as 100 we arrive at

If I had taken the figure for 1920 as it stood in the month of June or July, it would have shown a considerably higher level for that year and consequently the disparity would have been greater than is shown by the set of figures I have taken. In this table it will be noted that there is a difference of 33 points which means a decrease in the retail cost of commodities of approximately 18 per cent. It also means that the people who own the debt and control the money of the country are relatively so much better off to-day than they were in 1920. In other words, deflation which became effective in 1921 had the effect of adding more value to their holdings because the debt of this country was in no way affected by the deflation which then took place. The people who suffered mainly were the farmers, producers and working people. There is no need for me to mention the tremendous drop which took place in the price of farm commodities in those years. Hon. members of the farmers' group have referred to this matter on several occasions, but I would say that nothing would more forcibly show the feelings of the farmers of this country than the fact that in the election of 1920 they returned sixty-five members to this house. This no doubt was the result of the economic depression which hit the farmers so severely during that period. As regards the working people of this Dominion, in 1920 the number of wage earners was 526,571, and in 1921 this dropped to 381,203.
These are some of the results of the policy of deflation as adopted by the financial interests of this country. Whilst it left the great mass of the people poorer, these interests became more wealthy. When hon. members discuss the question of people leaving Canada, these figures might give one reason why so many men and women were compelled to emigrate. It was not choice but necessity that drove them away, and if such was the case, it is obvious where part of the blame lies.
The question arises why present and future generations should be penalized for the monopoly of money and currency by those who control it. Why should the taxpayers of Canada be penalized for things for which they are not responsible? Why should the government not use the power vested in them and adopt some measure that will protect and give back to the taxpayer that which has been taken away fro mi him by the hands of finance? My suggestion in this regard is that the amount of deflation as shown by statistics should also apply to the national debt. Why should the financiers of Canada and elsewhere benefit at
the expense of the great masses of the Canadian people? If the national debt were deflated in the same ratio as other commodities- and it is obviously fair that this should be done-the corresponding decrease would mean that the net debt of 1920 of 82,248,868,624 should be reduced by 18 per cent, which would mean that the figure for 1926 would be $1,844,072,272, or a reduction of $404,796,352. This in turn ought to save an annual interest charge, based on a rate of five per cent, of $20,239,800.
To create this deflation in the national debt,
I would suggest that Dominion currency equivalent to this amount should be issued over a period of three years and be used to retire bonded indebtedness. At the present time the Minister of Finance contemplates a loan of $500,000,000. How does the minister accomplish this? He issues securities which are regarded as gilt-edged, endorsed by the Dominion of Canada. These securities are easily negotiable and in many respects they have the same function as money, with this notable exception, that currency issued by the government bears no interest charges while bonds, of course, will. Naturally I would expect that bankers and other financiers would prefer to hold bonds which bear a good rate of interest to holding government currency which will not. It might be said that this suggestion would mean a policy of inflation. It would mean a policy of limited inflation of the currency of the country. What harm would it do? In place of creating any difficulty or doing harm, this limited increase in money issued by the Dominion government would be an advantage because in the first place it would mean a huge annual saving which, of itself, could finance the entire cost of the old age pension scheme for this Dominion. It would mean further that this extra money so created would have to find an outlet and this, in turn, would stimulate commercial activity. A policy of limited inflation must not be confused with the policy of inflation that was prevalent in European countries a few years ago. The amount of money and currency in circulation must always have a due regard to the productivity of the country, and I might also add to this, its potential productivity. Canada's industries have grown enormously since 1920, yet we find that the actual currency has decreased as shown in the following table:

The amount of currency issued by the Dominion treasury is very small as compared with the total amount of money in circulation in this country. As an example of the relation of currency to the total amount of money in circulation, it might be interesting to note the actual amounts on deposit in the chartered banks of Canada in 1920 and 1925, the last year for which statistics are available:

The total amount of currency for 1925 is equivalent to only ten per cent of the total bank deposits for the same period, and if the Dominion government added on to this currency an amount equivalent to the deflation between 1921 and the present year, it would naturally add a good deal to our currency, but even then it would be equivalent to only 26 per cent of the total deposits in our chartered banks.
Last year the hon. gentleman who now occupies the position of leader of the opposition (Mr. Bennett) made to the government a suggestion which they have filed away securely. It was that the government should conscript the surplus money owned by large financial institutions in this country and use it for the retirement of the national debt, paying four per cent for the use of same. I think that was a far more radical proposal than the one I am now suggesting. I had always thought, that, to the Conservative party, property was a sacred thing. At all events, I have not the least objection to the suggestion of the leader of the opposition, and I hope that he will repeat it during this debate. His proposal was regarded as a piece of statesmanship last year, coming from my hon. friend the leader of the opposition, but I suppose the same suggestion coming from this corner of the house would be regarded as bolshevism.
In the few minutes remaining to me, Mr. Speaker, I would like to say a word or two in reference to the closing remarks of the Minister of Finance. All through his budget address he had in mind the financier and the industrialist, and then practically in his last sentence he referred to the great masses of the people of this country, and his message to them was:	Work and be thrifty, I think he
had nothing else to offer them except that piece of advice. I am wondering who in this country does the work if it is not the working-

man and the man on the farm. Where else does all this prosperity come from? And then when you remember that the average man employed in industry in this country earns approximately only twenty dollars a week, I would like the Minister of Finance to tell the workingman where he is going to commence being thrifty on that wage, and where he is going to end. I would suggest to the Minister of Finance, when he talks about thrift, that he should start right on the government benches and set an example of thrift there. I am going to make a suggestion with which I hope our Conservative friends will agree. I would suggest that the Minister of Finance start saving on the militia estimates. These estimates show an increased appropriation of several million dollars over last year, and most of that money I presume will go in lace and gold braid. If there is a wasteful expenditure in any part of the world, it is this expenditure on armaments. When we have a delegate at the League of Nations, and a branch of the League of Nations Society in this country, with representatives going around and preaching peace among the nations of the earth, I think the last thing in the world the government ought to do is to increase the estimates for military purposes. I think it would have come with good grace from the Finance minister, if he had the least desire to set an example in thrift, to throw out these millions of dollars of increased expenditure in the militia estimates for this year.
With regard to the amendment placed in your hands, Mr. Speaker earlier this evening, by the hon. member for St. Lawrence-St. George, the one thing that seems to remain in my memory more than any other part of his speech is his reference to the Canadian National Railways. He referred in no complimentary way to the president of the Canadian National Railways, because he did not like something Sir Henry Thornton had said. When the hon. member for St. Lawrence-St. George does not like something which Sir Henry Thornton said, I am inclined to think that Sir Henry Thornton must have said a very good thing, because otherwise we would not find objections coming from the hon. gentleman. I cannot see that the amendment is any better than the budget itself. 1 think the speech which the hon. member for St. Lawrence-St. George gave this afternoon was the finest possible commendation of the budget I could have, and when I see commendation of the budget coming from the Conservative side of the house I am bound to feel a little bit suspicious of the budget myself.

The Budget-Mr. Harris

Anyone with common intelligence who finds it necessary to finance himself a little finds on going to the 'bank that while on the front of his statement he has to show' his assets, before he endorses that same statement he must give on the back all the notes or other securities which he has endorsed. That, in my humble judgment, is the course that should be pursued by this government, and I ask the minister to be frank and sincere with the people of Canada, and in future bring down a statement which will show the net debt with everything we have endorsed and for which we are undoubtedly responsible. As it is with the individual so it should be with the government.
In each budget presented by the minister we are told that our importations and our exports are of such a nature that we have a fine balance of trade, even though we find the imports creeping u,p a little. In that case the minister takes refuge in informing us that this increase is due to an increase of raw materials coming into Canada. But I ask the members of the house to look at and analyze the schedules prepared by the Department of Trade and Commerce; if they do this they must come to the conclusion that the increase in importations is not due to an increase in raw material, but is rather due in large measure to an increase in manufactured goods. So I desire to place on Hansard the facts with regard to several articles, since I have not time to review the whole schedule. These references, however, will illustrate the whole question, and a review of the schedule will confirm what ;I have to say. Let us consider first the non-ferrous metals, such as copper, silver, lead, zinc, cobalt and so on, which are found in raw state in abundance in this country. Taking the year 1924 as a basis,
we find that the increased importation of the manufactures of these materials amounted to 18.5 per cent in 1925, 28.4 in 1926 and 49.7 per cent in 1927. In that same period of four years, on the other side of the picture, see the exports of raw material of the same class extracted from the mines in Canada. Mr. Speaker, every time a train load of these raw materials goes to a foreign country to be manufactured you will find that from one to ten of the best workers of this country go also, to devote their energies to the manufacture of these goods and to produce the completed article, which will supply the home markets of the great industrial nation to our south, whose surplus will be returned to us and others in the form of fully manufactured goods. I say it is not fair to the artisans of our land and to our youth that this should be allowed to continue. It is not just; it is not right that those thousands graduating from our technical and commercial institutions should have to face these conditions and follow our raw material to a foreign land to find a vocation.
But we need not consider only the nonferrous group of metals. We will go a step further, and review the situation as it applies to iron and its products. That statement will not bear analysis.
