All these latter products, Mr. Speaker, as the hon. member for West Algoma fMr. Simpson) has said, we are able to manufacture to-day in our own steel mills.
Our Liberal friends were wont to go around the country preaching low tariff, and yet we find that the government are taking more money in customs duties this year than last by some $11,600,000. Our friends from the prairie provinces and some others who talk free trade say:	"Well, how can this be?"
They need only study the policy of the government to see how this seeming paradox is brought about. It will be found that on almost each and every occasion when they lower the duty on some manufactured article, simultaneously they see to it that all the parts which enter into the manufacture of that article are made subject to a lower duty. With what result? That some of our manufactories throughout the towns and cities which in years gone by have filled m slack time by manufacturing parts for a large concern now find themselves unable to compete against the influx of these parts from the United States. More and more of these parts are coming in, and more and more of our artisans find themselves out of employment. Then of course their only recourse is to migrate to the United States to find a livelihood. That is the reason why the minister this year expects to extract $11,600,000 more under the customs tariff than last year.
It is very interesting to note that the minister backed up his statement with regard to the importation of raw materials by giving some concrete examples. He told us that in 1921 we imported seven thousand auto engines whereas in 1926 we imported fifty-nine thousand. Some of my hon. friends who are interested in labour and know what an advantage it is to keep our artisans in the Dominion will find it instructive to estimate the number 56103-414
of artisans that might have been employed in this fair land of ours manufacturing those engines. In like manner, Mr. Speaker, as an example of raw material, mark you, coming into this country, the minister told us last year that auto parts to the value of six million dollars odd had been imported in 1921, whereas these imports had increased to over twenty million dollars in 1926. Again, I call attention to the fact that he terms these parts "raw materials". How many of our artisans would have enjoyed the privilege of working in the machine shops and foundries of their native country manufacturing that extra fourteen million dollars' worth of so-called raw material? The Minister of Finance in his budget speech backed up that ridiculous and unsound statement, so far as the facts are concerned, by saying that we were importing more and more raw material .to keep our factories busy I Last year he also drew attention to the fact that in 1921 we imported 7,784,980 pounds of raw wool, while in 1926 our importations had risen to 11,049,723 pounds. He took great pride in advising us that we had imported four million pounds more of raw wool in four short years. I see some of my farmer friends who perhaps know more about the sheep and wool industry than I do, but in all sincerity, Mr. Speaker, I ask since when have we convinced ourselves that we have not sufficient pasture land to produce from year to year millions and millions of sheep? Why is it that our sheep population dropped from 3,650,000 in 1921 to only a little over 2,500,000 this year? One reason is that we have imported four millions of pounds more of raw wool. The Minister of Justice seems to enjoy this, and even the Prime Minister, I notice, is very busy reading his paper. But what is he going to do with his own sheep? Not long ago I saw in the Star Weekly a picture of the Prime Minister tending his
The Budget-Mr, Harris

sheep. I wonder if he is going to put the sheep industry entirely out of business, and then find himself without a vocation during his summer holidays tending his sheep. We have 898,000 acres of pasture land ready for sheep to graze on, and instead our sheep population has decreased by one million in five short years. It should have increased by that number; and instead of our importations of wool having increased by four million pounds-and the minister taking pride in the fact-those importations should have decreased, and the product of our farmers should be competing with that of the farmers of other lands.
In like manner the Minister of Finance last year took pride in the fact that our importations of raw hides had risen from 22,000,000 pounds in 1921 to 42,000,000 pounds in 1926, and last year the figure reached 49,680,200 pounds. The average weight of a steer's hide is 50 pounds, which means that we are importing the hides of one million cattle. Yet the minister takes pride in the fact that our farmers are having their home market curtailed to that extent. The farmers of this country need some protection against the inroads of these raw materials, and in my humble judgment it is not good business for the minister to take pride in these disquieting facts, for they spell national disaster.
Last year the minister also put on Hansard figures showing the importations of leather unmanufactured, showing importations to the value of three million dollars odd in 1921, rising to $3,909,000 in 1926, and according to the figures this year given me by the Bureau of Statistics there has been a steady increase for the past year giving a total of $4,124,793. I ask the Minister of Customs-he is not in his seat I regret to observe-since when has it been necessary for us to import these tremendous quantities of leather, since when have our tanneries been unable to supply us with the leather that we need to manufacture into various articles? He comes from the good town of Kitchener where several of our largest tanneries are located, and it would be interesting to have his views on this subject.
The amount of money received from the customs tariff by this government has been augmented by the application of the antidumping clause, and also by placing on the reduced duty list those various parts which enter into the manufacture of all kinds of machines. The net result is that our factories, which a few short years ago were factories in the true sense of the word are now largely becoming assembling plants and distributing warehouses.

During the debate on the address, Mr. Speaker, I was interested to hear the Prime Minister enlarge on the great prosperity the country is enjoying due to the building boom in all the large centres of population. But if this boom is analyzed it will be found that of the eight hundred million dollars' worth of contracts he had in mind at least seven hundred million dollars' worth represented office buildings and hotels. What are these office buildings and hotels for; who are housed in them? They are chiefly for the accommodation of manufacturers' agents and others that come here to convince us that we should be buying their products instead of manufacturing our own. In addition to the office buildings the erection of new hotels is responsible to a large degree for this building boom. Why do we need new hotels? Simply to house the agents of foreign firms who come here to sell us the products of their factories. I see the Minister of Justice is enjoying this very much.

speechtext:
It has nothing to do with
the bag. The point is that the bag containing 50 kilos did not originate in England but at a continental 'point. Surely the minister knows that the English hundredweight is 112 pounds. I am sorry that in
order to illustrate my point I have to tell the minister that the English hundredweight is 112 pounds and the continental hundredweight 110 lbs.
On the whole, Mr. Speaker, I think the country is rather disappointed in the speech from the throne, in that there is too much said of an international nature, and not enough of a domestic nature. I fear that the government is leading us too far afield in our international relations, for we are too small in population to be dabbling in such affairs. The cost will steadily increase, and we already have sufficient evidence of this fact.
I do not think it is necessary for us to spend $225,000 this year in having diplomatic representatives in Tokyo, Paris and Washington. Instead of increasing our expenditure unnecessarily in this direction, in my judgment it would be much better to establish more trade commissioners throughout the world, as I have already tried to illustrate to the hon. Minister of Trade and Commerce. But apart from the mere expense, I say this dabbling in diplomatic services is fraught with great danger to this country. We have not the experience of a thousand years enjoyed by Great Britain. Much of her diplomtic skill to my mind is hereditary. Besides, Great Britain is backed by empire resources, she is backed by her navy; but we are backed by nothing on the sea. As long as we have the backing of the British navy, in my humble opiinon we shall enjoy another hundred years of peace. If we must spend this money, there are other and better ways of using it.
The time is too short for me to enumerate those channels of expenditure, but I am going to make one suggestion for the government to think over. This year I understand the government are going to bring down some legislation to give further effect to the Canada Highways Act. I hope that that legislation will be broad enough to embrace a fixed policy for the gradual elimination of level crossings on our highways. You are spending money under the Canadian Highways Act. See to it that it is spent in a way which will inure to the protection of the people by gradually eliminating level crossings. That is just one suggestion I have to offer in that connection.
Increased importation of goods of all kinds is bringing about a steady economic penetration of this country by the United States. The more our American friends penetrate this country and the more we buy of their materials the more and more dependent Canada will become upon the United States. I would prefer to see Canada more dependent on the British Empire than on the country to the
The Budget-Mr. Harris

south of us. Every time you open up a new embassy or establish more direct diplomatic representation in other countries you weaken the bonds which unite us with the motherland.
I have only about three minutes more to speak, and I shall have to draw my remarks to a close. Let me say to our friends from the western provinces that Ontario has given you of her sons and daughters, everything you asked for in the way of statutory freight rates, and other concessions of all kinds. In like manner let me say to our friends from the maritime provinces that we want to grant you almost anything that you like to ask us for in order that we may hold confederation together. We are spending money on your behalf under the Maritime Freight Rates Act, and we want to give you everything we can within reason. We are with you in demanding the full implementation of the Duncan report.
To our friends from Quebec I would say that I do not know of any other land where you would enjoy the freedom and privileges which you enjoy in Canada. I know that to-day your hearts bleed for those of your fellow countrymen who find themselves in Massachusetts and in the New England states generally. I know you want them all back, and so I say to you one and all: See to it that you adopt in this country of ours a policy that will provide employment for the minds and hands of all classes of people not only that unity may prevail in Canada but that we shall attain to that position in the future which a kind providence has set apart for us. I have much pleasure in supporting the amendment moved by the hon. member for St. Lawrence-St. George.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I am wondering what the people of Canada will be thinking to-morrow when they read the speeches of hon. gentlemen opposite which we 'have heard this afternoon. I was very much surprised to hear the remarks of the hon. gentleman who has just taken his seat (Mr. Harris) with respect to the city of Toronto from which he comes. If there is any city in Canada which has benefitted by the policy of the Liberal government during the last six years it is the city of Toronto.

speechtext:
If I understood my hon. friend aright he stated that the hotels built in Toronto were erected for the accommodation of foreign business agents. I would tell, my hon. friend those hotels were built to ac-{Mr. Harris.1
commodate the tourists that are coming from all parts of the United States to see the prosperity which prevails in Canada. That same tourist movement has been very beneficial in the province of Quebec.
The time allotted to me this evening, Mr. Speaker, will not permit me to follow in detail the remarks of the last speaker, but in answer to him, I will quote one whose opinion should be acceptable to my hon. friend from Toronto-Scarborough. I have before me a copy of the supplement to the annual financial review of the Toronto Globe of January 3, in which appears a statement from Mr. A. E. Ames, well known to all the Toronto members, reading as follows:
Retrospect of year 1927 shows large-scale progress throughout the Dominion.
An inventory of prosperity surpasses in proportion to population any other nation's-Canada's funded debt lowered-More income tax reductions seen advisable-Canadians spent fifty million dollars for foreign securities, and bought half domestic bond issues-Canadians in mood for real adventure-"Steady does it".
A cool retrospect of the year 1927 recognizes large-scale progress throughout the dominion. Perhaps the most notable features of the year in Canada have been the following, which are not intended to be listed in order of importance:
Reduction of federal funded debt in the last nine months by, say $42,000,000;
Increase in bank deposits of over $200,000,000;
Abundant harvests;
Notable development of hydro-electric power;
Important increases in paper and pulp making capacity;
Heavy increase in mining operation, construction and exploration;
General business prosperity;
A marked beginning of real estate activity, particularly in the larger cities.
That is the opinion of a gentleman in Toronto who is in a position fully to realize the great progress that Canada has made during the last six years. The Minister of Finance (Mr. Robb) is to be congratulated upon the budget which he has presented. Year by year we have seen the nation's prosperity increase until to-day we occupy, as a nation, one of the proudest positions in the world. That prosperity has not been confined to the cities but has been enjoyed by every class of our population. For the benefit of our western friends I should like to read an article from the same publication containing a statement by one who is known to them all. I refer to the Hon. T. A. Crerar, president of United Grain Growers:
During the past five years tile farmers of western Canada have produced and sold farm produce to the value of $2,000,000,000, taken at country points. Government statistics are not available with respect to all of this, but the government figures show the wheat crops alone in that time to have been worth almost $1,650,000.000 at country points, and to this is to be added the value of other crops, dairy products,

The Budget-Mr. Lapierre
live stock, and other products sold. These figures take no account of the enormous business in handling and transporting this produce, which would amount to many millions more.
Now, Mr. Speaker, we have had the opinions of those who are close to us, but I value very much more opinions from an independent source, and I have here the financial and industrial page of the Literary Digest, from which the following is taken:
In international trade, we are reminded, Canada now ranks fifth among the commercial nations of the world. A writer in The World's Work tells us that Canada's per capita wealth is excelled only by the United States and Great Britain, "being $2,406, compared with their $2,918 and $2,459, respectively." Roger W. Babson, we read further in The World's Work, has recently estimated that Canada leads the world in the number of homes owned by her own people, namely, 70 per cent.
For one thing, "the 2,278 miles of railway in 1867 have now been expanded to 40,352, and no country in the world has as large a railway mileage per capita."
"To-day", continues Mr. Stevenson, "Canada leads the world as an exporter of wheat, newsprint, nickel and asbestos, and her command of raw materials and water-power resources, which can cheapen the costs of the manufacturing processes, insures her steady industrial expansion."
This should be sufficient to meet the arguments that have been put forward that Canada is not to-day a prosperous nation.
As my time is limited, I should like to refer now to another item of the budget, which is much more interesting and which has not received during this debate the attention which it really deserves, having regard to its importance. During the discussions that have taken place this session reference has frequently been made to the visits to Canada last year of several distinguished personages, but there was one group which came to our country during 1927 whose visit had perhaps more to do with the future development of our mining resources than anything else that happened during that year. I have reference to the British Mining and Metallurgical Congress which met in Canada in 1927 and which was composed of some of the most eminent geologists, mineralogists and mining engineers in the British Empire. They were accompanied by a large number of distinguished men engaged in the same callings in different parts of the world. They were entertained and shown the wonderful mining resources which this Canada of our possesses.
I regret to say that the tremendous development of our mining resources is not receiving at the present moment the support and attention that it really deserves from the people of Canada. Our mining industry is one of the most hopeful features of our economic development. Canada possesses one of the most marvellous deposits of minerals in the
known world, and more than ninety-five per cent of the mineral wealth produced in this country has been produced within the last twenty-five years. That wonderful precambrian shield, which has often been referred to in this house, is one of the largest exposures of mother earth's natural wealth; containing 260,000 square miles, encircling Hudson bay and practically blanketing the whole of North America, it has already become one the largest producers of minerals in the world. In order that we may fully realize just how much this means in the future development of Canada I wish to cite a few figures which will, I am, sure, demonstrate to the satisfaction ol everybody that we are on the eve of one of the largest mineral developments the world has even known.
In 1927, the Dominion produced $243,000,000 worth of minerals, of which Ontario produced
$90,000,000. In Ontario the mineral production is as follows:
Gold	 $31,000,000
Nickel	 14,374,000
Silver	 5,760,000
Platinum	 1,000,000
Our tremendous mineral development will be realized when we remember that twenty-five years ago we had but one mine in northern Ontario; that in the last twelve months that northern country produced more than $32,000,000 worth of gold alone; that we now have in northern Ontario the second largest mine in the world, a mine which since 1921 has produced $121,000,000 worth of gold and distributed more than $50,000,000 in dividends. This is just the commencement of a new era; already new mines are being discovered throughout that northern section.
Let me describe the situation which exists in my constituency. We have in the Sudbury district, within a radius of ten miles, three of the most startling discoveries in the mining world. We are now producing 95 per cent of the world's nickel, and within the last few years discoveries have been made which promise to be of even greater value to Canada than our wonderful nickel deposits. We have in the Frood mine one of the largest copper deposits on the American continent; it is now estimated that there is on this property an ore reserve of more than 100,000,000 pounds of high class copper. When we stop to consider that this copper was localized through diamond drilling at the bottom of a nickel mine, assuring profitable mining for many years to come at greater depths, and when we consider that in nickel alone the mines that are now being operated have a reserve of ore for the next fifty or sixty years, we are just commencing to realize the value of our mineral products. To us who have
The Budget-Mr. Lapierre

waited all these years with faith in the future development of that mining country it was a source of the greatest satisfaction to hear those visitors from Europe express their astonishment that these tremendous mining deposits should have so long remained idle. They evinced the greatest interest in these wonderful deposits, and they were amazed at the variety of valuable minerals which are found within such a small area.
Another discovery which has been a revelation even to the oldest geologists and mining men in our section is that recently made in the centre of that great nickel deposit of one of the largest lead and zinc deposits on the American continent. This deposit means another producing mine in the centre of our nickel and copper country. The development work done' prior to the present assures us of a continuous supply of high grade lead and zinc ore for the next fifty years. We are assured of an expenditure of at least fifty million dollars for equipment, machinery and construction within the next two or three years. I need only refer to what has happened in my own part of the country. Those who have followed mining development in this country within the last few years must have heard of the great developments that have taken place in northern Ontario. There again we have a very wide area which is rapidly coming to the front as one of the largest producing areas on this continent. There has also been made recently a very interesting discovery in Manitoba, and to my friends from the west I would say that the development in the' northern section of that province would alone warrant the construction of two railroads to the Hudson bay. The amount of ore which has been exposed and is in reserve amounts to over four hundred million dollars. The ore blocked out or visible in the* Flin Flon, the Sherritt-Gordon and the Mandy mine assures for Northern Manitoba a development equal to that which we have seen in northern Ontario. Those of us who can remember twenty-five years ago when that entire area in northern Ontario, then given over to the lumber industry but today dotted with thriving towns and large productive areas of agricultural land, can draw a mental picture of what is going to happen in northern Manitoba. Every operating mine means a new settlement, the opening up of new agricultural land. It means a market close at hand for the farmer's products; it means the employment of thousands and thousands of Canadians in an industry that pays ample salaries and is a source of great wealth to any nation. These are some of the possibilities of the near future. We can 
see within the next ten or fifteen years an expansion in this country such as has not been seen in any other civilized countiy in the world.
Besides the minerals which I have mentioned we have as well very large deposits of iron ore. This is a question that will soon demand the attention of the government. The iron deposits of the lake Superior district of Michigan are now within calculable distance of exhaustion, and it will take but a short time before the ore reserves of that part of the United States will not be available for the Canadian market. We have at the present time several iron deposits which have been successfully operated. We have large deposits of siderite, which can be beneficiated, by which I mean any treatment which will remove the impurities or the sulphur and prepare the iron ore for the furnace. Our resources of iron ore are almost inexhaustible and the small margin that now exists between the price of the high grade Michigan ore and the low grade siderite and hematite ores that we have in northern Ontario assures us that the time is rapidly coming when these ores will be treated in this country, and that we shall have here an iron ore industry. What that will mean for Canada, what it will mean to our transportation problem,' and what it will mean to the future richness of the nation, can only be realized when we see what has taken place in the United States. Undoubtedly it will help us to solve our transportation problem. It will also help us to solve our unemployment problem, and it will add very largely to our national wealth. The development of these copper mines in northern Manitoba will mean a great deal to the industry all over Canada. For the treatment of these ores in Canada we' require a very large amount of machinery and equipment. Most of that equipment at the present moment can be and is being manufactured in Canada; in fact, the activity which has been quite noticeable within the last few years in the mining equipment business and allied industries is due entirely to the mining development that has taken place.
We must bear in mind that the future of the mining industry depends very largely upon foreign capital. For years our mines remained undevolped for want of capital. I have heard some severe criticism and some doubts expressed as to the wisdom of attracting American capital to develop our Canadian mines. Mining differs in a great many ways from ordinary business. It is a business that is more or less speculative; it is a business of great hazards, and only those who are in

The Budget-Mr. Dickie
the business and have successfully developed mines are inclined to invest the immense amount of capital required to develop a mine. As I said a moment ago, the International Nickel Company in the installation of plant and equipment necessary to develop their new copper deposits will spend in the neighbourhood of fifteen to eighteen million dollars. There are very few corporations and very few individuals who are disposed to invest such a large amount of capital in an enterprise in connection with which they will have to wait possibly five or six years for any returns. That, Mr. Speaker, accounts in very large measure for the large amount of foreign capital which is coming into our mining areas. We would have welcomed a great deal more of English capital, but, unfortunately for us, the first English corporations which came to Canada and invested in our mines were unfortunate in their selections. They came into the mining area before the geology had been thoroughly explored, but to-day those areas are coming into their own. The holding in Canada of the 1927 convention of the mining congress has demonstrated to those learned men what great mineral deposits there are in this country.
The mining industry is one of those activities which unfortunately attracts but little attention, Though it is but rarely referred to in this house it is pregnant with wonderful possibilities for the future development of this country. It is predicted by those who are best in a position to know that within the next decade the products of our mines will be our largest source of wealth. We in the north have hope and faith in the future of this nation. We have seen the rapid transformation which has taken place in that part of Ontario, and we can see that with the continuous increase in the productivity of the west, with our industrial expansion due to the development of the natural resources and our increasing world trade, in the near future, Canada will be called upon to take her place among the leading industrial nations of the world.

speechtext:
I am sure we alii listened with great interest to the address of the hon. member for Nipissing (Mr. Lapierre). We were very glad to hear of the wonderful progress which has been made in the north country, and I am sure the indomitable people who first went in there deserve all the success which they will doubtless achieve. There is a wonderful mining country in northern Ontario; another is coming into being in Manitoba, and we have the mines of Quebec as well. Wherever the Laurentian shield extends minerals will be
found, and wherever the precambrian rocks exist will be found gold. The geologists tell us that in two years Canada will outstrip the United States, and that in less than five years we will produce more gold than South Africa. That is a wonderful tribute to a wonderful country.
We also have great mines in British Columbia, among them the biggest copper mine and the biggest lead mine in the British Empire, and in British Columbia mining is also experiencing a revival. Canada has great forests, immense potential waterpowers and wonderful agricultural land, and the sad thing is that with all these possibilities we are drifting along, lagging behind with a population of only nine million people. There is something wrong with the directorate of this country or we would not have this state of affairs. Look at the situation with regard to our forests: each year wood, wood products and paper to the value of $240,000,000 go to the United States; we export to the markets of the world a great quantity of grain; we have these great mineral deposits. Why then, are we simply marking time while other nations outstrip us in the race for nationhood? I think we should devote a little more attention to economics and waste less time worrying about our status within the British Empire. We should make a sound economic study of this country, but I am afraid the present government is unfit for the task.
It was a pleasure to listen to the last speaker (Mr. Lapierre), but it was painful to listen to the budget speech this year. The minister fulfilled a very difficult task, but he presented a very serious aspect of affairs when we come to analyze it. Canada is not going ahead as she should. We say times are better here, and that everyone in Canada is prosperous. That may be so to a certain extent, but if you ask two or three thousand people in this beautiful little city whether they have experienced any prosperity, and ask the same question in Vancouver, Montreal or Toronto, I am quite sure they will all tell you the same thing. We cannot be a prosperous nation unless the rank and file are prosperous, and unless people are employed. Why are they not employed? Why are they going to the United States year by year, as has been the case ever since I can remember? Our manhood and womanhood are the only finished products the United States will accept from us, and they take our young men and women without question because we are known to be a resourceful, honest people. They would rather swell their population with Canadians than perhaps any other race on the face of the earth. I can remember that in the early days in California the best recommendation
The Budget-Mr. Dickie

any man could have was to be a Canadian, and almost the same situation exists there today. As I have said, we were known to be resourceful: we were accustomed to frugality and were not given to many of the habits which prevailed in that careless western country, so people wanted Canadians in their employ if they could possibly get them. At present in the cities of Seattle, Portland, San Francisco and Los Angeles, I venture to say one-half the bank employees are Canadian boys who have drifted down from Vancouver Island, and their fondest wish is that some day they may be able to return. Of course they cannot go down there under contract to work, but they write to a manager of a bank to ask if he requires any additional help. They will then receive a letter telling them to call in if they happen to be going past the bank, and when they do so almost invariably they secure employment at wages much better than those paid by Canadian banks.
We speak of an immigration policy; let us get right at the root of the matter and see on what we can found such a policy. There is only one sound principle, and that is to make this country a place where workingmen can exist and rear their families in comfort. Let us provide an outlet for our children, so that when they graduate from the universities and commercial schools they will be able to find employment and remain in the country they love so well. As it is now, what prospect is there for any of these men in the west, let us say? They are all raising families, only to see them depart for the United States as soon as they attain manhood and womanhood. That can be prevented by making this country just as good to live in as they find the United States. We still have plenty of raw material, although we are waging a relentless fight against our forests. The forests of the United States, together with a good many mines, have become nearly exhausted; as you all know, there is very little pulpwood left in the eastern United States. If we do not continue our foolish policy of sending them $15,000,000 worth of pulpwood every year, their paper mills will have to close down and they will probably come to Canada to carry on the manufacture of paper. I say we can make this country as attractive as the United States; it could be done if we had the proper directorate, but today, when we should be riding on the crest of the wave of prosperity, we find ourselves wondering whether times really are good in Canada.
What have we been doing; what has been our policy? After looking over the figures I wonder that we find ourselves as well off as
[Mr. Dickie. 1
we are. Let us consider the trade of Canada with the British Empire. In 1926 our exports to the United Kingdom amounted to about $459,000,000, while in 1927 they fell to 8409,000,000, in round figures. That represented a loss of $50,000,000 in our exports in one year. In 1926 we imported from the United Kingdom goods to the value of $164,000,000, roughly, and in 1927 about $182,000,000, which meant that we imported $17,000,000 more in goods and exported $50,000,000 less. In 1926 our favourable balance of trade with the United Kingdom was about $299,000,000, while in 1927 that figure fell to about $217,000,000. That represented a loss in trade of $82,000,000, although of course we still have a very favourable trade balance with the United Kingdom. Bearing in mind that $217,000,000, let me give the figures with reference to our imports and exports. From the United States in 1926 we imported goods to the value of $668,000,000, and in 1927, $707,000,000. There we have an increase. In 1926, on the other hand, we exported $465,000,000 and in 1927, $474,000,000. That may not seem very bad on the face of it, but our unfavourable balance of trade in 1927, compared to 1926, shows a loss of trade of $39,000,000. We received $217,000,000 from the United Kingdom of a favourable balance in our trade, whereas we paid to the United States $232,000,000 more than we received from our friends in Great Britain. In other words, our balance from the United Kingdom is wiped out completely and we have to dig down into our pockets for sufficient money to offset the difference in respect of the United States.

speechtext:
Yes, but a trade that is
unfavourable to Canada. Were it not for the products derived from our diminishing forests, forests that are being rapidly depleted, we should have an unfavourable balance of trade with the United States such as would alarm even my hon. friend from East Calgary (Mr. Adshead). I can understand a gentleman of my hon. friend's point of view wishing to buy

The Budget-Mr. Dickie
from the United States where he can buy on the cheapest terms; and that possibly is a good argument for a western man if he has no desire to do anything for Canada as a whole. But surely the people of this country, we in this House of Commons, should view the Dominion as an entity and be prepared to make some compromises for the common good. I believe we can make times good in Canada and build up manufactures in Ontario and Quebec, and also make Winnipeg and Calgary manufacturing cities. But in order to do this our people must cultivate the spirit of compromise. Is it not worth it to bring about a state of things whidh will make a home for our children when they have graduated from our schools, rather than have them drift away from us to enhance the prestige and enrich the coffers of the country to the south of us?
I have no fault to find with the policy of the United States; indeed, I only wish that we in Canada would copy it. I can well remember the time when the United States imported from England all the iron and steel it required. England had built up an admirable manufacturing industry in this line through the employment of the best scientists in the world. And she had coal and iron ore lying side by side, sufficient to supply the demands of all nations for iron and steel. At that time she supplied the needs of the United States in this direction. But what happened? Broadminded men in that country saw that too much money was leaving the United States, and they took this view:	"We have the raw
materials; let us build up an iron and steel industry in this country. Let us supply our own needs." But people with small minds who did not view things with a broad outlook said, "You will have to pay more for your iron and steel." Well, those of foresight in the United States admitted this, but they pointed out that they would be able to provide employment for a larger population. With this object in view the United States imposed an almost prohibitive duty on iron and steel, increasing it still higher until the duty conr stituted practically an embargo. And under that embargo was built up the great iron and steel industry of the United States, the barometer of trade in that country. Armies of men were employed in the iron and coal mines; cities sprang up; thousands of people came from other countries, and a vast population was accumulated. What argument was there against the means which they adopted to build up that industry, which could not have been created unless the people had been willing to pay more for their product for a time at least? When they had their industry in full working order then they were able to compete with the world in iron and steel.
But it took them many years to accomplish this. Now, I have no doubt that we could do the same in Canada if we only tried. We need to use good judgment in considering the question, but I see no reason why my hon. friend from East Calgary, and for that matter any gentleman living say in the interior of Saskatchewan, should lose one dollar through the development of trade in this manner. I can conceive the possibility of a government with actuarial ability and broad common sense quite easily devising some scheme whereby if one part of the country suffered unduly by reason of something that made for the prosperity of the Dominion as a whole the discrimination might be offset in gome compensatory way. I see no reason why this should not be done.
I know no argument that can be advanced against a larger population for Canada; certainly we must have a population. But as things are being carried on in Canada at the present time I dislike seeing any immigrant come to these shores. Let us get the country ready for immigrants; let us so arrange our economic affairs that if a man, for some reason or other, cannot take up farming he may go into some manufacturing centre and find work not only for himself but for his children as well. A policy of this sort requires sensible, careful handling, and above all we must look at things from a broad national standpoint. Let us take pride in this great country, about which we have heard from my hon. friend who preceded me. Let us see whether we cannot make this nation worth while. I have not the slightest doubt that with a sound economic policy we could bring millions of people here to augment our population, having them knocking at our doors for admission.
We are spending millions of dollars to induce immigrants to come into Canada while at the same time the Americans are spending vast sums to keep them away from their country. Canada for the last twenty-five or thirty years has been an immigration agent for the United States; I make that statement without the slightest fear of contradiction. The very best of our young men have been pouring across the border year after year, with the result that while the Americans are securing all the immigrants they can assimilate we are losing the cream of our population. So rapidly, indeed, is the population of the United States increasing that that country has found it necessary to enact a quota law to keep foreigners from its shores. Our Canadians, on the other hand, are admitted into the United States without let or hindrance. Why can we not take a leaf out of their book? Why can
The Budget-Mr. Dickie

we not adopt some sound, vigorous policy which will promote our own interest? We need not be bound by mere words; let us shun the term "'protection" and "free trade" and simply get down to a common sense basis. Let us enact some common sense legislation which will foster various enterprises in this country. In may be perhaps that under some form of protection a manufacturer here or there may profit unduly. But we can take steps to remedy any evil that may arise in this direction. Nevertheless I am firmly of the belief that our manufacturers must be protected if we are to get anywhere; they must be enabled to make such profits as will render it possible for them to pay fair dividends, to lay by something against lean years, and to pay their employees as good wages as are paid in the United States, and even better.
Give our manufacturers Canada for a market and they can do this; and we can see to it that they do not profiteer to any unreasonable extent. As things are to-day, our industries are fighting against odds: the boot and shoe manufacturers and the textile people are Struggling along, not knowing what they will do from day to day. The textile industry of Canada supplies ju'st thirty per cent of the wants of our people, working only fifty-eight per cent of single shift time. And the same condition exists in other industries; the cloth industry is in serious straits to-day. It may be asked: What about the textile industry of the United States? It also is in bad shape; it is not making any profits. But the situation is entirely different in the United States. Over there they have ninety per cent of the home trade in addition to the trade they secure from Canada. The industry in the United States is over-machined; it has too much equipment. We in Canada on the other hand have an equipment which is sufficient to supply the needs of a far larger market than we enjoy at the present time; we could supply 75, 80 or 90 per cent of the people of Canada with cloth if only the conditions were favourable.
I might discuss other industries but I will not do so; the story is very largely the same in respect of them all. We must give our manufacturers a chance tc make good. Do not let us think that every manufacturer, because he makes a profit, is diabolical, as I have heard him characterized on the floor of this house. Our manufacturers must make money. There must be some goal for them to strive towards, otherwise they will not invest in industrial enterprises in Canada. With our wonderful water-powers, and with

natural resources such as we have in this country, Canada should be highly prosperous. Let us see whether we cannot ride on that wave. I have every sympathy with the people both of the province of Quebec and of the prairies. Indeed, so far as the prairie provinces are concerned, all you have to do is to visit that country in the winter and you will realize the conditions that confront those people. Possibly they are not living the kind of life that makes for a broad point of view; conditions there may have a tendency toward narrowness of view.

Nevertheless, they are conditions that make for honesty of purpose. I give the people of the west credit for that virtue.
In conclusion, may I ask that we forget everything but, the important fact that we are all Canadians living in a great country which we can make still greater, a country of which we should all be proud? Let us not give up to politics that which was meant for mankind. And too many of us are inclined to do this. I mentioned the people of Quebec. Let me say, so far as they are concerned, that they are a fine industrial people who are willing to work, and it is unfortunate that for years and years their population should have been drifting across the line. As a good old priest remarked to me one day, "When our people go across the border away from mother church they lose the religion they learned at their mother's knee." Why should this be necessary? Quebec, with its wonderful resources, should be able to retain all its population and repatriate manjr of those who have left the Dominion to help to make the United States a great nation. Let us do something to remedy this condition of affairs.

subsubtopic: DEBATE ON ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
This is
practically the first time, Mr. Speaker, I have addressed the house, because I had not an opportunity to speak in the previous debate. However, I will now take occasion to make a few remarks on the motion before the house, and before discussing the subject matter of the present debate I wish to congratulate you, Mr. Speaker, on the manner in which you have presided over the deliberations of this chamber. I do not want to throw bouquets or burn too much incense, but I think I may safely say that your presence is an invaluable asset to the house.
I would also congratulate the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) on the splendid document we have in the speech from the throne, now disposed of, while at the same time commending the mover and the seconder

The Budget-Mr. Dionne
of the address in reply thereto. Let me also compliment the leader of the opposition (Mr. Bennett) on his elevation to the position he now holds. It is a matter for gratification that the members on this side of the house show such good will and understanding in the support they give to the government, while I admire at the same time these qualities in hon. gentlemen opposite, who support their chief with equal loyalty. And while I am offering congratulations, I must not forget the ministers of the government, who have so wisely managed the affairs of the country.
As a member from Quebec, I rejoice in the elevation of Archbishop Rouleau to the office of cardinal, and as one interested in the diocese of Rimouski I take very great pleasure indeed in the appointment of Bishop-elect Courchesne.
Now, Mr. Speaker, I do not intend to review all that has been said since the beginning of the session; interesting though it would be, I have no inclination to travel all over the globe following ail those who in their speeches have been making excursions into other countries. We have heard a good deal about emigration and immigration. As regards emigration, I have read that the Chinese at one time built very high and thick walls around their country and erected ponderous iron gates to keep the insiders in, but after a number of years they were obliged to remove the gates and very largely demolish the walls to let those insiders out. I presume it was getting too warm from overcrowding, and now the Chinese are scattered pretty nearly throughout the entire world. It is a very difficult matter, Mr. Speaker, to prevent emigration; indeed, it is almost an impossibility. But emigration can be to some extent moderated by means of -laws not only enacted but strictly enforced.
As regards immigration, we have been acquiring considerable experience over the years, not without some success, and at a considerable expenditure. I am in favour of immigration, but I do not think that we should restrict it to people from the British Isles; we should get immigrants from France, Belgium and Sweden. When we are discussing the types best suited to this country, surely we must realize that the peasants from these three countries are well adapted indeed to conditions in Canada; they are farmers who have been brought up to an agricultural life and they would certainly do well here. What we need is, of course, an increase of population; our population instead of being nine or ten millions should be anywhere from seventy-five to a hundred millions. It is all very well to aim at an increase in population by means
of immigration; but, Mr. Speaker, what is far more desirable is a natural increase. I would advocate the marriage of men between the ages of twenty and forty-five, and if we could raise families of five, ten and fifteen, yes, and even twenty children, our immigration problem would soon be solved. I would even encourage the marriage of the youngsters, those between eighteen and twenty. These youngsters marry, it is true, but unfortunately they ignore the responsibilities of the married state and have no children.
Coming now to the budget, I must congratulate the Minister of Finance (Mr. Robb) on the very able speech he delivered to the house. In view of what that speech discloses, there is not only hope of prosperity; we are actually in an era of prosperity. Agriculture is our main industry in Canada and we should encourage it by every means at our disposal. The farmers deserve every assistance we can give them. I have heard a good deal about the development of our natural resources, and much has been said in regard to mines, minerals and ores. This is all very well, but we must have the courage to develop those resources.
I have here a newspaper despatch quoting the comment of the London Express on the Robb budget:
The Budget Makes One's Mouth Water
London, 20 (S.P.A.). The newspaper "The Express" commenting on the Robb budget, says that it is one of those which makes one's mouth water. It is a further proof that Canada is one of the most enviable countries of the world, and that its prosperity, born from its natural resources, is permanent. After all. this is but a small issue if we are to compare it to the future possibilities which awaits it. Young men and girls should have no hesitation. The inheritance of the Empire and of good fortune await them on their arrival."
The Sunday Observer remarks that Mr. Robb prepared his budget in view of rousing the envy of the finance ministers of Europe. "The tariff" it states, is of a nature to safeguard the interests of the country in a movement which is making great progress. The principle of British preference is always maintained and is established as solidly in Canada as it is in England. In a word the budget and the conclusions which they draw from it show up the opportunities of an energetic and coherent policy of immigration.
Now I return to the subject of immigration. There are some sons of Canada that have been in the United States for a number of years and they would be happy to return to this free country. By all means let us encourage the repatriation of Canadians now resident in that country. Some of them may not be able to come back, but others will be very glad to settle cun farms in this Dominion. At the same time while it is a good thing to encourage immigration, it is far better to
The Budget-Mr. Dionne

keep in Canada those who are now here. Hon. gentlemen opposite have spoken of the exodus to the United States, and they say it should be checked. By all means let it be checked. I remember, however, the period from 1882 to 1896, although I was very young then, when the Conservatives were at the head of affairs in this country. There was quite an exodus to the United States at that time, and what did the government of that day do to check it? Absolutely nothing.
I am not going to enter, Mr. Speaker, upon the discussion of the complicated tariff items dealing with woollens, textiles, silks, worsteds and so on. The hon. member for St. Law-rence-St. George (Mr. Cahan) undertook that task this afternoon and got considerably twisted in his subject. I should not like to meet with the same experience.
Hon. gentlemen opposite talk about the national policy. Their policy used to be "Liberal-Conservative"; now they have dubbed it " national." It will only be necessary to add i-s-t for it to become " nationalist."
Some hon. members have spoken here about the banking system. The banking system in this country is all right enough; it works fairly well for those who can get money from a bank, but the farmer cannot get it. So far as he is concerned the system is no good. I will not speak about capital, because since 1925 I have been more used to paying interest than accumulating capital. I will not speak about capitalism because I know nothing about it. What I am familiar with is capitalized interest. Neither will I venture an opinion with respect to capitalists. I know some of them and they are very nice, decent " socialists."
Talking about repatriating Canadians from the United States, there is a nice opportunity for promoting this laudable movement. I refer to the building and operating of a railroad from Gaspe to a point in the Mate-pedia valley and then on to Edmundston. This line would run through a well timbered territory, through country rich in minerals. There are rivers and lakes in that district which would prove a paradise to the sportsmen. I do not hesitate to say that tourists would pour in by the thousands to that district if it were made accessible. Here is an opportunity to settle repatriated Canadians, along the route of this new railway. It would help in the opening up of new parishes, and would develop the natural resources of this part of Canada, to say nothing of yielding millions of feet of lumber and millions of cords of pulpwood. Taking

all the prospects into consideration, this railway, if it were built, would in my opinion, be one of the most profitable in the whole country.
Something has been said about encouraging the raising of sheep. Now that sheepskins are entering into the manufacture of furs of
all kinds, here is an additional incentive for the raising of sheep.
I should like to say a word or two to those who fear the occurrence of another war. There is a cloud in the sky, but it not a cloud which portends danger. It is a cloud full of good will and understanding, if I may use that expression, and it will burst in an expression of good will over the entire world. Let there be no fear of the coming of another war. If one should occur it will not be fought with deadly weapons but with pop-guns and peashooters.
I have already spoken of the natural resources which await development in my constituency. There are wharves also which need filling, and I hope the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Elliott) whose generosity is so well known, will make generous expenditures for this purpose, not only in my constituency but in other constituencies also. May I say in conclusion that I trust the government will not exercise the pruning knife too rigidly when it comes to making provision in the supplementary estimates for works of various kinds calculated to meet the necessities of the community and to promote in every way the development of the country. I hope to have other opportunities of explaining the needs of my constituency.

While it is a little earlier than usual to rise, there was an understanding between the whips that upon the conclusion of the speech of the hon. gentleman who has just resumed his seat, the debate should be adjourned. I therefore move the adjournment of the debate.
Motion agreed to and debate adjourned.
On motion of Mr. Mackenzie King the house adjourned at 10.10 p.m.
